title: I love speed. We all love speed. But what happens when the speed is slowing you down?
author: Sonny DeSorbo
text:
Back to Articles

I love speed. We all love speed. But what happens when the speed is slowing you down?

Community Article Published
September 13, 2026 Upvote 3 Sonny DeSorbo darkc0de
When comparing large language models, we usually reduce the discussion to two questions:
Which model is smarter?
And:
Which model is faster?
But for many real-world applications—especially autonomous agents, coding agents, research systems, and tool-using assistants—neither question actually tells us which model will perform the most useful work.
The better question is:
Which model reaches a correct result fastest?
That sounds like a minor distinction, but it changes the way we should think about model architecture, quantization, benchmarks, and even the meaning of "performance."
A slower model may be substantially more intelligent per inference. A faster model may compensate for weaker reasoning by making several attempts in the same amount of time. A higher-precision quantization may generate tokens more slowly but make fewer mistakes, eliminating entire correction cycles.
The optimal model is therefore not necessarily the smartest model or the fastest model.
It is the model with the best time-to-correct-result.
Intelligence and Speed Are Different Resources
Consider two current Qwen models.
Qwen3.8-27B is a dense 27-billion-parameter model. Qwen describes it as designed for stronger coding, reasoning, professional work, and long-horizon agentic execution. Its official results include 89.2 on GPQA Diamond, 90.3 on LiveCodeBench v6, and 79.5 on IFBench.
Qwen3.5-35B-A3B is a very different design. It contains roughly 35 billion total parameters, but it is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with only about 3 billion parameters activated for each token. Qwen explicitly designed this architecture for high-throughput inference with relatively low computational cost.
Its published results include 84.2 on GPQA Diamond, 74.6 on LiveCodeBench v6, and 70.2 on IFBench.
The benchmark methodologies are not identical enough to claim that these numbers constitute a perfectly controlled head-to-head experiment. But together with Qwen's description of Qwen3.8 as a substantial capability improvement, they support the reasonable conclusion that Qwen3.8-27B is generally the more capable reasoning model.
That still does not automatically make it the better model for every workload.
Qwen3.5-35B-A3B only activates approximately 3B of its 35B parameters on each token. Qwen3.8-27B is dense. On hardware and inference engines that exploit the MoE architecture effectively, the difference in generation speed can therefore be enormous.
Suppose, purely as an example, the dense model takes 60 seconds to attempt a task.
The MoE model takes 15 seconds.
Now suppose Qwen3.8 has an 85% probability of completing the task successfully on its first attempt, while the smaller-active-parameter MoE succeeds only 65% of the time.
At first glance the 85% model looks like the obvious choice.
But the MoE model can potentially make four attempts during the dense model's first attempt.
If the environment gives the agent useful feedback—compiler errors, failed unit tests, tool responses, browser state, validation errors, or other signals—the second attempt is not necessarily another blind 65% gamble. The model can learn from what went wrong.
It might fail.
Read the error.
Modify its approach.
Fail again.
Read the new error.
Correct itself.
And finish successfully before the more intelligent model has completed its first generation.
That is a fundamentally different kind of performance.
From Intelligence to Intelligence per Second
For interactive agents, raw intelligence is only one component of capability.
A useful simplified metric is:
Expected Time to Success = Time per Attempt / Probability of Success per Attempt
If Model A takes 60 seconds and succeeds 90% of the time:
60 / 0.90 = 66.7 seconds expected time to success
If Model B takes 20 seconds and succeeds 60% of the time:
20 / 0.60 = 33.3 seconds expected time to success
Under this simplified model, the substantially less reliable model still gets the job done roughly twice as quickly.
Real agents are more complicated because attempts are not independent. In fact, this often strengthens the argument for speed.
A coding agent does not have to erase its memory after a failed attempt. It can see that a test failed, inspect the traceback, modify three lines, rerun the test, and continue from there.
The first failed attempt produced information.
So the useful unit of computation is not simply accuracy per generation.
It may be closer to:
progress toward a validated solution per second.
This is one reason extremely fast models can punch above their apparent benchmark class when placed inside a competent agent harness.
The Qwen3.8 vs. Qwen3.5 MoE Problem
This makes a comparison such as Qwen3.8-27B versus Qwen3.5-35B-A3B much more interesting than asking which model scores higher on benchmarks.
For a difficult one-shot question with no external verification, I would generally favor Qwen3.8-27B.
There is no guarantee that anyone will catch an error. More attempts do not help if the system does not know the first answer was wrong.
For an autonomous software-development agent, however, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B may sometimes become much more competitive.
The environment itself can serve as a critic.
The code compiles or it does not.
The unit tests pass or they do not.
The webpage rendered correctly or it did not.
The API returned the expected object or it did not.
The agent therefore has access to something enormously valuable: cheap objective feedback.
Speed lets it exploit that feedback repeatedly.
This produces a counterintuitive situation in which the theoretically less capable model can have greater effective capability per unit of wall-clock time.
There is a limit, of course.
If the weaker model fundamentally cannot solve the problem, allowing it to fail ten times faster merely produces ten failures. Speed can compensate for an elevated error rate; it cannot compensate indefinitely for missing capability.
This means there is an intelligence threshold for every task.
Below that threshold, speed is nearly irrelevant.
Above it, speed can become extremely important.
Quantization Creates the Same Problem Inside a Single Model
An even cleaner example appears when comparing different quantizations of the same model.
Consider Qwen3.8-27B at Q4_K_M versus Q5_K_M.
Q4_K_M stores the model at lower precision and normally requires less memory bandwidth. Q5_K_M retains more information from the original weights but increases memory consumption.
The general llama.cpp quantization data illustrates the tradeoff clearly. In its reference measurements, Q4_K_M produces greater quantization error than Q5_K_M, while requiring fewer bits per weight. For one published test model, Q4_K_M showed a perplexity increase of approximately 0.175 over the baseline compared with approximately 0.057 for Q5_K_M.
The speed difference is hardware-dependent rather than universal. On memory-bandwidth-constrained systems, smaller quantizations can be meaningfully faster because fewer bytes must be moved for every generated token. llama.cpp measurements have demonstrated this relationship directly, including configurations where Q4_K_M generated faster than Q5_K_M.
So which one should a coding agent use?
Again, tokens per second is not enough.
Imagine Q4_K_M completes an average attempt in 40 seconds while Q5_K_M requires 50 seconds.
Q4 is 20% faster.
But suppose Q4 succeeds on 72% of the tasks and Q5 succeeds on 90%.
Their expected times become:
Q4_K_M: 40 / 0.72 = 55.6 seconds
Q5_K_M: 50 / 0.90 = 55.6 seconds
They are effectively tied.
That gives us a useful break-even rule.
For two versions of the same model:
Q4 wins when:
P(Q4) / P(Q5) > T(Q4) / T(Q5)
If Q4 takes only 80% as long to run as Q5, it can tolerate roughly a 20% relative reduction in success probability before its speed advantage disappears.
This is much more useful than saying "Q5 is smarter" or "Q4 is faster."
Why Coding Makes Precision More Valuable
There is another complication.
Not all failures cost the same amount.
Suppose Q4 produces code 20% faster but introduces slightly more subtle errors.
A syntax error is cheap. The agent immediately sees it and corrects it.
A wrong variable name is cheap.
A failed unit test is relatively cheap.
But an architectural mistake may cause the agent to spend five additional iterations modifying code built on a bad assumption.
A silent logic error can be worse still. The program runs, the agent thinks it succeeded, and the error survives validation.
In that environment, a very small increase in model quality can generate a disproportionately large reduction in total runtime.
This is where Q5_K_M can potentially become faster by being slower.
Suppose Q4 writes its initial patch in 45 seconds.
It fails.
It spends 20 seconds reading the error and generating another patch.
Another test exposes a different problem.
Another 25 seconds are spent fixing it.
Total: 90 seconds.
Q5 takes 55 seconds to produce its initial patch.
It passes.
Total: 55 seconds.
Measuring generation speed alone would have declared Q4 the winner.
Measuring end-to-end task completion produces the opposite result.
Failure Amplification
This effect becomes increasingly important as tasks become longer.
A chatbot response might involve one reasoning chain and one answer.
An autonomous coding task could contain hundreds of decisions:
Understand the request → inspect repository → select files → understand architecture → write code → call tools → compile → test → diagnose → modify → test again → review.
An error near the beginning can propagate through everything that follows.
That means model reliability can have a compounding effect.
A 3% reduction in the probability of making the correct choice at any single step does not necessarily produce a 3% worse agent. Across a long trajectory, it can produce substantially more failed branches, backtracking, tool calls, and repeated generation.
This is why quantization losses that appear almost insignificant on conventional language-model benchmarks can matter more in long-horizon agents.
Conversely, it is also why speed matters so much. When errors are easily observable and recoverable, rapid iteration can neutralize much of that disadvantage.
The workload decides which effect dominates.
There Is No Universal "Best Quant"
This also explains why statements such as "Q4_K_M is the best quantization" are useful rules of thumb but not universal laws.
Q4_K_M is popular precisely because it occupies an attractive part of the size-quality tradeoff. But the best format depends on the task and the hardware.
For casual conversation, Q4 may be an obvious choice.
For high-volume summarization, faster inference may dominate.
For brainstorming, multiple fast generations may actually be more useful than one higher-fidelity generation.
For a coding agent, Q5 may be worth the cost if the increase in reliability removes enough correction loops.
For mathematical reasoning where there is no automatic verifier, preserving additional model quality becomes still more attractive.
For an agent operating a computer with strong environmental feedback, a faster model may regain the advantage.
And if Q5 fits entirely in VRAM while Q4 does as well, their real-world speed difference may be small enough that there is little reason not to use Q5.
If Q5 causes partial CPU offloading while Q4 remains entirely GPU-resident, the situation can reverse dramatically.
The model does not exist separately from the machine running it.
The Missing Benchmark: End-to-End Useful Work
Most LLM benchmarking still separates quality and performance.
One benchmark reports reasoning accuracy.
Another reports coding capability.
An inference benchmark reports tokens per second.
A quantization test reports perplexity degradation.
Those numbers are useful, but users ultimately care about something combining all of them.
For agents, a more meaningful benchmark would give every model the same set of tasks, the same tools, and the same maximum wall-clock budget.
Then measure:
How many tasks did the system successfully complete before the clock ran out?
A dense model might solve 8 of 10 tasks with almost no retries.
A small MoE might solve only 6 of 10 on its first attempt but ultimately complete 9 because it can iterate three times as quickly.
A Q4 model might generate 25% faster but spend 40% more time correcting itself.
A Q5 model might execute fewer tokens but finish more actual jobs.
That would tell us considerably more about practical model performance than either benchmark accuracy or tokens per second in isolation.
A Proposed Benchmark: Persistent Challenge Completion
The benchmark should go one step further than measuring whether a model can solve a task within a fixed number of turns. It should test whether the model can continue working intelligently until it succeeds, while respecting a fixed wall-clock budget.
Call this benchmark Persistent Challenge Completion, or PCC.
The central rule is simple:
Give the model a difficult, objectively verifiable task and require it to keep going until it succeeds or the time budget expires.
The model is not judged on its first answer. It is judged on whether it can make progress, interpret feedback, recover from failure, and eventually produce a validated result.
Task Design
Each task should include:

A natural-language objective.
A controlled environment.
A fixed set of available tools.
An objective success validator.
A maximum wall-clock budget.
A reproducible starting state.
A record of all actions, outputs, failures, and retries.

Coding tasks are the clearest starting point. A task might ask the agent to modify an unfamiliar repository, implement a feature, repair a bug, migrate an API, or improve performance while preserving existing behavior.
Other domains could use the same structure:

Data analysis tasks with hidden validation queries.
Browser tasks with state-based success conditions.
Research tasks with citation and fact-checking validators.
Mathematical tasks with executable proof or symbolic verification.
Infrastructure tasks with deployment and health checks.
Tool-use tasks involving APIs, files, databases, or simulated environments.

The benchmark should deliberately include tasks that are difficult enough to produce failures. If every model succeeds immediately, the benchmark measures one-shot capability rather than persistence.
The Persistence Protocol
At the beginning of each task, the model receives the objective and the available tools. It may inspect the environment, form a plan, and begin acting.
After every meaningful action, the environment returns the same feedback that a real agent would receive:

Compiler output.
Test results.
Validation errors.
Tool responses.
Browser state.
Runtime logs.
Resource or permission errors.
Explicit success signals.

The model must then decide what to do next.
It may revise its plan, inspect more files, undo a change, try a different approach, or continue testing. It is not allowed to declare success without passing the validator.
The run ends when:

The task passes the objective validator.
The wall-clock budget expires.
The model reaches a predefined safety or resource limit.
The model explicitly gives up.

The benchmark should not impose an arbitrary retry count. A fast model should be allowed to make more attempts, while a slower model should be allowed to spend more time reasoning per attempt. The fixed resource should be wall-clock time, with token usage and tool calls reported separately.
Primary Metrics
The primary metric should be Validated Work per Second:
VWS = Number of successfully completed tasks / Total wall-clock time
For a fixed benchmark suite and time budget, this can be reported as:
Completion Rate = Successful tasks / Total tasks
and:
Time to Success = Wall-clock time from task start to validator success
The most important aggregate should be the area under the completion curve. At every point in time, record how many tasks have been completed. A system that completes many tasks early should score higher than one that completes the same number only at the end of the budget.
A useful normalized score is:
PCC Score = (1 / N) × Σᵢ (B − tᵢ) / B
where:

"N" is the number of tasks.
"B" is the maximum time budget.
"tᵢ" is the time at which task "i" was successfully completed.
Unsolved tasks receive a score of zero.

This rewards both completion and speed. Completing a task at the beginning of the budget earns more than completing it just before the deadline.
The benchmark should also report:

First-attempt success rate.
Final success rate.
Median and percentile time to success.
Number of retries.
Number of tool calls.
Tokens generated.
Tokens per successful task.
Failed-task recovery rate.
Fraction of failures that were detected by the agent.
Fraction of detected failures that were successfully repaired.
Silent failure rate.
Resource consumption and cost.

Measuring Persistence Rather Than Random Repetition
A benchmark of this kind must distinguish useful persistence from blind repetition.
Repeatedly submitting the same broken patch should not count as intelligent iteration. The environment should therefore record whether successive attempts make measurable progress.
Possible progress signals include:

More tests passing.
Fewer compiler errors.
Reduced validator distance.
More required files or components correctly configured.
Improved objective score.
Fewer failing assertions.
Successful completion of previously failing subtasks.

The benchmark can report a Progress Efficiency metric:
Progress Efficiency = Validator improvement / Wall-clock time
A model that fails but steadily reduces the remaining error should be distinguished from one that produces unrelated or repetitive attempts.
The harness should also detect loops. If the agent repeats substantially identical actions without improvement, the run can continue for fairness, but the behavior should be reported as a persistence failure rather than a success strategy.
Difficulty Tiers
The benchmark should contain several difficulty tiers.
Tier 1: Local correction
The task has a clear error message and a short path to repair. This measures whether the model can use direct feedback.
Tier 2: Multi-file implementation
The task requires repository exploration, architectural understanding, and several coordinated changes.
Tier 3: Ambiguous debugging
The visible failure is indirect. The model must form hypotheses, design experiments, and identify the underlying cause.
Tier 4: Long-horizon engineering
The task requires planning, implementation, testing, refactoring, and recovery across many steps.
Tier 5: Adversarial or deceptive validation
The task includes misleading symptoms, hidden tests, edge cases, or conditions where a superficial solution appears to work.
A model should not receive a high persistence score merely by solving easy tasks repeatedly. The benchmark should report a completion curve across difficulty, showing the highest task complexity at which the system can reliably finish within the budget.
Controlling the Agent Harness
To compare models fairly, the benchmark must separate model capability from harness capability.
Every model should receive:

The same system prompt.
The same tool definitions.
The same context limits.
The same environment.
The same task order or randomized task assignment.
The same maximum wall-clock budget.
The same validator.
The same permissions and resource limits.

The harness should not silently provide model-specific prompting or retries.
At the same time, the benchmark should support two tracks.
The standardized-agent track uses one fixed harness for direct model comparison.
The optimized-system track allows developers to tune prompts, memory, planning, tool selection, and retry policies, but requires publishing the complete configuration.
This distinction matters because the benchmark is ultimately about systems, not isolated model checkpoints. A model with better memory management or a more effective verification loop may produce more useful work even if its raw generation quality is unchanged.
Preventing Benchmark Gaming
The validator must be hidden or difficult to exploit. Visible tests alone can encourage agents to hard-code expected outputs or optimize for superficial signals.
Tasks should therefore include:

Hidden tests.
Randomized inputs.
Multiple valid solution paths.
State checks that cannot be satisfied by a fake response.
Reproducible but undisclosed edge cases.
Validation after the agent terminates.

The benchmark should also verify that the final artifact, not merely the model's explanation, satisfies the objective.
For coding tasks, this means running hidden tests against the resulting repository. For browser tasks, it means checking the final application state. For research tasks, it means evaluating claims against a hidden reference set. For mathematical tasks, it means executing a proof checker or symbolic validator.
Reporting the Speed-Quality Frontier
The benchmark should not collapse every result into one number.
For each model and configuration, publish a frontier showing:

Completion rate at several time budgets.
Median time to success.
First-attempt accuracy.
Final success after persistence.
Cost per successful task.
Token and tool usage.
Failure and recovery behavior.

This makes it possible to see whether a model is:

Strong but slow.
Weak but fast.
Good at detecting and repairing errors.
Good at one-shot solutions but poor at recovery.
Capable of persistence but prone to unproductive loops.
Highly reliable but inefficient.
Fast enough to compensate for lower first-attempt quality.

A single leaderboard number can hide these differences. A completion curve reveals them.
Why This Benchmark Would Change Model Selection
Suppose Model A solves 70% of tasks on its first attempt and Model B solves only 50%.
A conventional benchmark would rank Model A higher.
But after thirty minutes of persistent interaction, Model A might complete 75% of the tasks while Model B completes 90% because Model B is fast, uses feedback effectively, and can make many more attempts.
Alternatively, Model B might complete only 55% because its failures are not recoverable. The same first-attempt score can therefore produce very different system outcomes.
This is precisely the behavior that current static benchmarks fail to capture.
The benchmark would also expose quantization tradeoffs that perplexity and tokens-per-second measurements miss. A Q4 model might have lower first-attempt accuracy but a higher completion rate under a generous time budget. A Q5 model might dominate under short budgets because it avoids expensive correction loops. The crossover point would become measurable rather than speculative.
Most importantly, the benchmark would reward models that know how to use failure.
A model that treats an error message as useful evidence is more valuable than one that merely generates a plausible first answer. A model that can abandon a bad plan is more valuable than one that repeats it confidently. A model that verifies its own work is more valuable than one that stops after producing an attractive-looking artifact.
The Benchmark's Hardest Requirement
The phrase "keep going until it succeeds" sounds simple, but it creates a difficult evaluation problem.
Persistence must not mean endless activity. The model should continue when additional work has a reasonable chance of improving the result, but it should also recognize when its current strategy is failing.
A strong persistent agent should be able to:

Detect that an attempt failed.
Identify what evidence caused the failure.
Update its internal hypothesis.
Choose a materially different corrective action when necessary.
Preserve useful progress.
Revert harmful changes.
Allocate time between investigation and implementation.
Stop only after success is verified or the remaining budget is no longer useful.

This suggests a second metric: Recovery Quality.
Recovery Quality can be estimated from the conditional probability that a model succeeds after an initial failure:
Recovery Quality = P(success within budget | first attempt failed)
A model with modest first-attempt accuracy but excellent recovery quality may be ideal for interactive environments. A model with high first-attempt accuracy but almost no ability to recover may be better for one-shot tasks.
The benchmark should make both properties visible.
A More Complete Performance Equation
The original simplified equation can therefore be expanded.
For a persistent agent, useful performance depends on:
Validated Work per Second = Successful Outcomes × Value per Outcome / Wall-clock Time
But successful outcomes depend on more than first-attempt probability. They depend on:

Initial capability.
Generation speed.
Tool latency.
Feedback quality.
Error detectability.
Recovery quality.
Planning quality.
Context retention.
Probability of entering unproductive loops.
Cost of each failure.
Remaining time after each failure.

A more realistic conceptual model is:
P(success by time B) = f(I, Q, S, F, R, C, B)
where:

"I" is task-solving intelligence.
"Q" is output quality and reliability.
"S" is inference and action speed.
"F" is the quality of environmental feedback.
"R" is recovery ability.
"C" is the cost and complexity of failure.
"B" is the available time budget.

There is no universal ordering of models under this function. The winner depends on the task distribution and the environment.
The Fastest Model Is Not Always the Fastest Model
This produces two conclusions that initially sound contradictory.
A weaker but dramatically faster model can outperform a stronger model because it has enough time to attempt, observe, correct, and attempt again.
At the same time, a slower and higher-quality model can outperform a faster version because it avoids those correction cycles entirely.
Both are true.
The deciding variable is not token generation speed.
It is the cost of failure.
When failures are cheap, obvious, and easily corrected, speed becomes extraordinarily valuable.
When failures are difficult to detect, cause cascading mistakes, or require expensive backtracking, reliability becomes more valuable.
And when a task exceeds the weaker model's fundamental reasoning ability, no practical amount of additional tokens per second will save it.
So instead of asking:
What is the smartest model I can run?
Or:
What is the fastest quantization I can run?
The better question is:
Which configuration produces the greatest amount of validated, correct work per unit of time?
That is the performance metric that matters.
Not intelligence alone.
Not quality alone.
Not speed alone.
Intelligence per second—and ultimately, successful work per second.
Don't take any if this too seriously, just sharing an AI powwow session.
